a-simple-model-of-the-atom-symbols-relat.d: A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes
terms: The smallest part of an element that can exist. All substances are made of atoms.
A substance made of only one kind of atom. There are about 100 different elements, shown in the periodic table.
The one- or two-letter code used to represent an atom of an element, eg O represents an atom of oxygen and Na represents an atom of sodium.
The table in which the elements are shown; it is supplied in the exam.
A substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions, represented by a formula built from the symbols of the atoms it was formed from.
A change that always forms one or more new substances and often involves a detectable energy change. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
A representation of a reaction using the names of the reactants and products, with an arrow from reactants to products.
A representation of a reaction using symbols and formulae in which there are the same numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
(HT only) An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, eg 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
(HT only) An equation showing only the ions and atoms that take part in the reaction, with spectator ions left out.
Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together; the chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.
A physical process that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; the solid stays on the filter paper as residue and the liquid passes through as filtrate.
A physical process in which the solvent is evaporated from a solution so that the dissolved solid is left behind as crystals.
A physical process that separates a solvent from a solution by boiling it off and condensing the vapour, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
A physical process that separates two or more miscible liquids using the differences between their boiling points.
A physical process that separates substances in a mixture by how they move with a solvent through paper.
A separation method that involves no chemical reaction, so no new substances are made.
An idea used to explain observations; new experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.
The model that followed the discovery of the electron: the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus is charged.
The model in which the mass of the atom is concentrated in a small charged nucleus; it replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, in which electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances; his calculations agreed with experimental observations.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus; the positive charge of a nucleus is a whole number of these identical charges.
An uncharged particle in the nucleus; the experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons, about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.
A negatively charged particle, relative charge −1, that occupies energy levels (shells) around the nucleus.
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.
Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
The centre of the atom, containing almost all of its mass, with a radius less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m).
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so the numbers of protons and electrons are no longer equal.
An average value for an element that takes account of the abundance of its isotopes.
A region around the nucleus that electrons occupy; electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells) first.
The arrangement of electrons in the energy levels of an atom, written as numbers such as 2,8,1 for sodium or drawn as a diagram.
The arrangement of all the elements in order of atomic (proton) number, set out so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column.
A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and so have similar chemical properties.
A row of the periodic table. The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in an atom of the element.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It fixes the element's place in the periodic table.
The electrons in the highest occupied shell of an atom. Their number decides the group and controls the element's chemical reactions.
The repeating of similar properties at regular intervals along the order of elements, which is why the table is called periodic.
The mass measure used to order elements before subatomic particles were known; now called relative atomic mass.
Spaces left in his table for elements he believed had not yet been discovered, with properties predicted from the neighbouring elements.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, which is why atomic weight does not always rise with proton number.
An element that reacts to form positive ions. Metals lie to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table.
An element that does not form positive ions. Non-metals lie towards the right and top of the periodic table.
An ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.
The elements of Group 0. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable electron arrangements.
An outer shell holding eight electrons, or two in the case of helium, so the atom has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
Boiling points increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down the group.
The elements of Group 1. Their characteristic properties follow from the single electron in the outer shell of their atoms.
The alkaline compound produced, along with hydrogen, when a Group 1 metal reacts with water.
Reactivity increases going down the group, as the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost.
The elements of Group 7. They are non-metals with seven outer electrons whose atoms go about in pairs as molecules.
A molecule made of two atoms joined together, the form in which the halogen elements exist, such as Cl2 and Br2.
The ionic compound formed when a halogen reacts with a metal, such as sodium chloride or iron bromide.
The covalent compound formed when a halogen reacts with a non-metal, such as hydrogen chloride.
Reactivity decreases going down the group, as the outer shell is further from the nucleus and an electron is gained less easily.
A reaction in which a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen in an aqueous solution of its salt.
The metals in the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3. They have properties that are similar to one another and different from the properties of the Group 1 metals.

The metals in the first column of the periodic table, such as lithium, sodium and potassium. They are soft, have low melting points and low densities, and react quickly with water, with oxygen and with the halogens.

Transition elements have much higher melting points than Group 1 metals. Chromium melts at about 1907 degrees C and iron at about 1538 degrees C, while sodium melts at about 98 degrees C and potassium at about 63 degrees C.

Transition elements are much denser than Group 1 metals. Copper is about 8.9 g/cm3 and nickel about 8.9 g/cm3, while sodium is about 0.97 g/cm3, which is less than the density of water, so sodium floats.

Transition elements such as chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel are hard and strong, which is why they are used for tools, machinery and hard-wearing chrome plating. Group 1 metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife.

Group 1 metals react with cold water, fizzing as hydrogen is released. Transition elements react very slowly or not at all with cold water, which is why copper is used for water pipes and why iron only rusts slowly in damp air.

A freshly cut Group 1 metal loses its shine within seconds as it reacts with oxygen in the air. Transition elements react far more slowly: copper stays shiny for months, and only turns black when it is heated strongly in air.

Group 1 metals react vigorously with the halogens. Transition elements react much less readily and usually need heating: hot iron reacts with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride, 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3.
Many transition elements form more than one ion. Iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+, copper forms Cu+ and Cu2+, and chromium forms Cr2+ and Cr3+, whereas a Group 1 metal only ever forms a 1+ ion.

Compounds of transition elements are usually coloured: copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) sulfate is pale green, iron(III) oxide is red-brown, nickel(II) compounds are green and potassium manganate(VII) is purple. Group 1 compounds are usually white and give colourless solutions.

A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up in the reaction. Many transition elements and their compounds are catalysts: iron in the Haber process, nickel for hardening vegetable oils, and manganese(IV) oxide for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

The Roman numeral in a name such as iron(II) chloride or manganese(IV) oxide gives the charge on the metal ion, not the number of atoms in the formula. Iron(II) chloride is FeCl2 and iron(III) chloride is FeCl3.

chemical-bonds-ionic-covalent-and-metall.d: Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic
terms: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. All three are electrostatic in origin, but they differ in which particles are held together and in what happens to the outer electrons.
Bonding in which the particles are oppositely charged ions. It occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. It occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons. It occurs in metallic elements and in alloys.

The force of attraction between opposite electric charges. Chemical bonding is explained by electrostatic attraction: between positive and negative ions, between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons, or between metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
The movement of electrons from the outer shell of a metal atom to the outer shell of a non-metal atom when the two react. Transfer produces ions; it is not itself the bond.
An ion formed when a metal atom loses one or more electrons from its outer shell. It has more protons than electrons, so its charge is positive.
An ion formed when a non-metal atom gains one or more electrons into its outer shell. It has more electrons than protons, so its charge is negative.
The full outer shell arrangement of a Group 0 element. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
A diagram that shows the electron transfer forming an ionic compound, using dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for the other, so that the origin of each electron can be followed.
For the elements in scope, the charge on the ion follows from the group number: Group 1 forms 1+, Group 2 forms 2+, Group 6 forms 2- and Group 7 forms 1-.
An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions, held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. There are no separate molecules in it.
In an ionic lattice the electrostatic forces act in all directions, not along a fixed line between two chosen ions. This is what is meant by ionic bonding.
The structure of sodium chloride can be shown as a two-dimensional diagram, as a three-dimensional ball and stick model or as a space-filling model. Each is a model of the same giant lattice.
Empirical formula of an ionic compound
The simplest whole number ratio of the ions in the structure. It is worked out from a model or diagram by counting the ions of each type and cancelling to the simplest ratio.

A ball and stick model shows gaps between ions that do not exist and sticks that are not real; a two-dimensional diagram shows forces in only two directions; no diagram can show the full extent of the lattice.

When atoms share pairs of electrons they form covalent bonds, and these bonds between atoms are strong. The strength of the bonds inside a molecule says nothing about the melting or boiling point of the substance.
A covalently bonded substance may consist of small molecules, each containing a small fixed number of non-metal atoms, such as H2, Cl2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2.
A covalently bonded substance whose molecules are very large: many small molecules joined into long chains. A polymer has very large molecules, not a giant structure.
A structure in which very many atoms are joined by covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, with no separate molecules. Diamond and silicon dioxide are the specification's examples.
Dot and cross diagram of a molecule

A diagram showing the shared pairs of electrons in a molecule, using dots and crosses to show which atom each electron came from. Required for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane.
A polymer is represented by its repeating unit drawn in brackets with a subscript n, where n is a large number. It is not a value to be calculated from the diagram.
In a displayed formula or a diagram of a giant structure, one line between two atoms represents one single covalent bond, that is one shared pair of electrons.
A dot and cross diagram shows the electrons but not the shape or size; a two-dimensional diagram flattens a three-dimensional molecule; a ball and stick model exaggerates the space between atoms.
The molecular formula is deduced by counting the atoms of each element shown in the model or diagram. The bonds, sticks or lines are not counted, and the number is not reduced to the simplest ratio.
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.

An electron from the outer shell of a metal atom that is no longer held by one atom and is free to move through the whole structure. Sharing these delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
A mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements. The bonding in an alloy is metallic, as it is in a pure metallic element.

how-bonding-and-structure-are-related-to.d: How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances
terms: The state in which particles are packed closely in a fixed arrangement, so a solid keeps its own shape and volume.
The state in which particles are still close together but can move past one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
The state in which particles are far apart and move randomly, so a gas fills whatever container it is put in.
The one temperature at which a substance melts and at which it also freezes. Solid to liquid and liquid to solid both happen at this temperature.
The one temperature at which a substance boils and at which it also condenses. Liquid to gas and gas to liquid both happen at this temperature.
Simple model of the three states
A model in which the particles of a substance are represented by small solid spheres, arranged closely and regularly in a solid, closely but randomly in a liquid, and far apart in a gas.
The attractions holding the particles of a substance to one another. Their strength depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.
The energy that must be supplied to separate particles from one another. The stronger the forces between the particles, the more energy is needed and the higher the melting point and boiling point.
(HT only) In the simple model there are no forces between the particles, all particles are shown as spheres, and the spheres are shown as solid.
A property such as melting point, colour, hardness or electrical conductivity that belongs to a large collection of particles arranged in a structure, not to a single atom.
The letter or letters written in brackets after a formula in a chemical equation to show the state of that substance: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid and (g) for gas.
A solution made by dissolving a substance in water. It is shown in an equation by the state symbol (aq).
The regular structure formed by an ionic compound, in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in a repeating three-dimensional arrangement.
The attraction between oppositely charged ions. In a giant ionic lattice these forces are strong and act in all directions.
High melting and boiling points of ionic compounds
Ionic compounds melt and boil at high temperatures because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds in the lattice.
When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water the ions become free to move, so charge can flow and the substance conducts electricity.
A substance whose particles are small groups of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Such substances are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting and boiling points.
The weak force of attraction between one molecule and another. It is these forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.
A strong bond formed by a shared pair of electrons between two atoms inside a molecule.
Molecules are neutral, so a molecular substance has no charged particles that are free to move and it does not conduct electricity.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
A substance whose molecules are very large. The atoms in a polymer molecule are joined to other atoms by strong covalent bonds, usually forming a long chain.
Why polymers are solids at room temperature
Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.
A structure in which all of the atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. These bonds must be overcome to melt or boil the substance.
Diamond and graphite, which are forms of carbon, and silicon dioxide, also called silica.
The strong bonding in the giant structure of atoms that makes up a metal. It means that most metals have high melting and boiling points.
Layers of atoms in a pure metal
In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers. The layers can slide over one another, which allows metals to be bent and shaped.
A mixture of a metal with other metals. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed to make alloys, which are harder.
Electrons in a metal that are free to move through the whole structure. They carry electrical charge through the metal, so metals conduct electricity well.
Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred through the metal by the delocalised electrons.
A substance is solid below its melting point, liquid between its melting point and its boiling point, and gas above its boiling point.

A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure. Diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.

A structure in which a very large number of atoms are joined to their neighbours by strong covalent bonds that run right through the substance. There are no separate small molecules, so there are no weak forces between molecules to overcome.

Every carbon atom in diamond is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds, in a rigid three-dimensional network. No atom can be pushed out of position without breaking covalent bonds, so diamond is very hard.
Why diamond has a very high melting point
Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking a very large number of strong covalent bonds. This takes a great deal of energy, so the melting point is very high.
Why diamond does not conduct electricity
Each carbon atom in diamond uses all four of its outer electrons to form covalent bonds. There are no delocalised electrons, so there is nothing free to move through the structure and carry charge.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

The hexagonal rings of graphite are joined into flat layers, and there are no covalent bonds between the layers. The layers are held to one another only by weak forces of attraction, so they can slide over each other.

In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised. Because each atom uses only three of its outer electrons in covalent bonds, the fourth is not held on one atom and is free to move through the structure, carrying charge and thermal energy.
Why graphite is soft and slippery
There are no covalent bonds between the layers of graphite, so whole layers can slide over one another. Layers rub off easily, which is why graphite leaves a mark on paper and can act as a lubricant.

One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so these electrons are free to move through the structure. Moving electrons carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity, and they also carry thermal energy.
Why graphite has a very high melting point

Within each layer the carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. A very large number of these strong bonds must be broken to melt graphite, so the melting point is very high even though graphite is soft.
How graphite is similar to a metal

Graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons. These delocalised electrons let graphite conduct electricity and thermal energy in the way that the delocalised electrons of a metal do, although graphite is a non-metal whose atoms are joined by covalent bonds.

A single layer of graphite: one sheet of carbon atoms, each joined to three others by covalent bonds in hexagonal rings, one atom thick. Graphene has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.

Because graphene is a single layer of graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so graphene conducts electricity, which makes it useful in electronics. Every atom in the sheet is held by strong covalent bonds, so graphene is very strong for its mass, which makes it useful in composites.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
The first fullerene to be discovered, C60, which has a spherical shape.

A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio, which means the tube is extremely long compared with how wide it is. Their properties make carbon nanotubes useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.

Fullerenes are hollow, so other molecules can be held inside the cage, which is used to deliver drugs into the body. They have a large surface area, so they can be used as catalysts, and they are also used as lubricants. Carbon nanotubes are used in nanotechnology and electronics, and are added to materials to reinforce them, for example in tennis racket frames.

Graphene is drawn or described as a single flat sheet of hexagonal rings, one atom thick, with no layers above or below it. Fullerenes are drawn or described as closed hollow shapes, a ball or a tube, built mainly from hexagonal rings and sometimes containing rings of five or seven carbon atoms. Graphite is drawn as several such sheets stacked in layers.

bulk-and-surface-properties-of-matter-in.d: Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)
terms: The study of structures that are 1 to 100 nm in size, which is of the order of a few hundred atoms. Nanoscience deals with structures far larger than a single atom but far smaller than anything visible under a light microscope.
A particle 1 to 100 nm across, that is 1 x 10⁻⁹ m to 1 x 10⁻⁷ m. Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles, so they are the smallest of the three particle sizes named in this section.
Particles with diameters between 100 and 2500 nm, that is between 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. They are larger than nanoparticles and smaller than coarse particles.
Particles with diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m, so from 2500 nm up to 10 000 nm. Coarse particles are often referred to as dust, and are the largest of the three sizes.

One thousand-millionth of a metre: 1 nm = 1 x 10⁻⁹ m. A nanometre is one millionth of a millimetre, and a micrometre (1 x 10⁻⁶ m) is a thousand nanometres, so the three particle sizes span from 10⁻⁹ m up to 10⁻⁵ m.

The total surface area of an object divided by its volume. For a cube of side x the surface area is 6x² and the volume is x³, so the ratio is 6x² divided by x³, which is 6 divided by x. The ratio therefore depends only on the size of the cube, not on how much material there is in total.
Effect of size on the ratio

As the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10 the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces leaves the total volume unchanged while the total surface area rises, which is why very small particles have very high ratios.

Nanoparticles may have properties different from those for the same materials in bulk because of their high surface area to volume ratio. The material is chemically the same; it is the very large proportion of its atoms that sit on a surface, rather than any change of substance, that makes it behave differently.
Because of the high surface area to volume ratio, smaller quantities of a nanoparticulate material may be needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.
Nano dimensions against atoms and molecules

An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m), so an atom is about 0.2 nm across and a small molecule is a fraction of a nanometre. A 1 nm nanoparticle is therefore only a handful of atoms wide, and a 100 nm nanoparticle roughly 500 atoms wide - which is why 1 to 100 nm structures contain of the order of a few hundred atoms.

Nanoparticles have many applications in medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts. New applications for nanoparticulate materials are an important area of research.

Using the information you are given, weigh the advantages of the nanoparticulate form (often that it works better, or that far less material is needed) against the disadvantages and risks, and then give a judgement that follows from that comparison. An evaluation that reports only one side is not an evaluation.

There are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles. Their effects on health and on the environment have not been fully investigated: they are small enough to be breathed in or to pass into cells and the bloodstream, and they are washed into the environment from products such as sun creams and deodorants. Long-term effects are not yet known, so more testing and research are needed.
Why bulk safety data is not enough

A material that is safe to handle in bulk is not automatically safe as nanoparticles, because nanoparticles may have properties different from those of the same material in bulk. The risk has to be assessed for the nanoparticulate form itself rather than assumed from the bulk material.

chemical-measurements-conservation-of-ma.d: Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations
terms: The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
A representation of a reaction using chemical formulae, with the reactants on the left of the arrow and the products on the right.
A symbol equation in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the equation, which is what conservation of mass requires.
A number written in normal script before a formula, which multiplies every atom in that whole formula. In 2Ca(NO3)2 the leading 2 doubles the entire formula unit.
A small number written after a symbol, or after a closing bracket, which multiplies only the atom or the bracketed group that it immediately follows.
The relative mass of an atom of an element, the building block from which a relative formula mass is assembled.
The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
In a balanced chemical equation the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum of the relative formula masses of the products in the quantities shown.
The share of a compound's relative formula mass contributed by one element: the Ar of that element multiplied by the number of its atoms, divided by the Mr of the compound, then multiplied by 100.
A reaction vessel open to the surroundings, so a gaseous reactant can enter or a gaseous product can leave without being weighed on the balance.
Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate
Heating breaks the carbonate down into the metal oxide and carbon dioxide; the carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.
Particle model explanation of a mass change
An account of an apparent mass change in terms of gas particles entering the vessel from the air, or leaving it and dispersing among the particles of the air.
The doubt that always exists about the result of a measurement, present whenever a measurement is made, however good the apparatus and the technique.
The pattern formed by a set of repeated measurements, showing where the results cluster and which of them lie apart from the rest.
A measurement lying well outside the cluster formed by the others; it is spotted when the distribution is represented and is excluded from the mean.
Range as a measure of uncertainty
The difference between the largest and the smallest of a set of measurements, used about the mean as a measure of uncertainty and quoted as the mean plus or minus half the range.

use-of-amount-of-substance-in-relation-t.d: Use of amount of substance in relation to masses of pure substances
terms: The unit in which chemical amounts are measured; the symbol for the unit mole is mol. A label such as '0.50 mol of sodium chloride' states a chemical amount, not a mass and not a volume.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass. One mole of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) has a mass of 100 g; one mole of H₂O (Mr = 18) has a mass of 18 g.
Equal amounts, equal numbers of particles

One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles - atoms, molecules or ions - as one mole of any other substance. Equal amounts in moles therefore mean equal numbers of particles, however different the masses are.
The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance. Its value is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole. It is a number of particles per mole, not per gram.

Amounts in moles can be applied to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations. In one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂), although one mole of CO₂ contains three moles of atoms.
The number of moles in a given mass is found by dividing that mass in grams by the relative formula mass: number of moles = mass ÷ Mr. 20 g of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) is 0.20 mol.
The mass of a known amount is found by multiplying the amount in moles by the relative formula mass: mass = number of moles x Mr. 0.25 mol of MgCl₂ (Mr = 95) has a mass of 23.75 g.
The masses of reactants and products can be calculated from balanced symbol equations. In a closed system the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants that reacted.

Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ shows that one mole of magnesium reacts with two moles of hydrochloric acid to produce one mole of magnesium chloride and one mole of hydrogen gas.

The balancing numbers in an equation give the ratio of the amounts in moles of the substances involved. They do not give the ratio of the masses, because each substance has its own relative formula mass.

To find the mass of one substance from the mass of another: convert the known mass to moles using its Mr, apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then convert back to a mass using the Mr of the substance wanted.

The balancing numbers in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products by converting the masses in grams to amounts in moles and converting the numbers of moles to simple whole number ratios.

The amounts in moles are divided through by the smallest of them, and multiplied up if needed, so that the balancing numbers are the simplest whole numbers that fit. 0.2 : 0.1 : 0.2 becomes 2 : 1 : 2.
A relationship can be rearranged to make any of its quantities the subject. From number of moles = mass ÷ Mr come mass = number of moles x Mr and Mr = mass ÷ number of moles.
A reactant supplied in more than the amount the equation requires. Using an excess of one reactant makes sure that all of the other reactant is used up.

The reactant that is completely used up in a reaction. It is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products: the amount of product is worked out from the amount of the limiting reactant, not from the reactant in excess.
The concentration of a solution measured as mass per given volume of solution, for example grams per dm³ (g/dm³). A concentration of 20 g/dm³ means 20 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution.
Mass of solute in a given volume
mass of solute = concentration x volume of solution, with the volume in dm³. Because 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, a volume given in cm³ is divided by 1000 before it is used.

Concentration depends on both quantities: for a fixed volume of solution, more solute gives a higher concentration; for a fixed mass of solute, a larger volume of solution gives a lower concentration. Adding water to a solution therefore dilutes it.

yield-and-atom-economy-of-chemical-react.d: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
terms: The mass of product that would be obtained if every one of the reactant particles reacted in the way the balanced equation shows and none of the product was lost. It is the largest mass that could possibly form, so it is the figure the actual mass is compared with.
The amount of a product obtained from a reaction. It is the amount actually made and collected, measured after the product has been separated from the reaction mixture.
The yield compared with the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage. It measures how much of the possible product was actually obtained in that particular preparation.

% Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100. The mass actually made goes on the top and the maximum theoretical mass on the bottom, so the answer can never exceed 100%.
Reversible reaction as a reason for a lower yield
The reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible. Reactants are still present when the amounts stop changing, so less product forms than the equation predicts.

Some of the product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example crystals left on filter paper, solution left in a beaker, or solid left behind on transfer. The product still exists, but it is not weighed.
Some of the reactants may react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming products other than the one wanted. Those atoms are then unavailable for the desired product, so its yield falls.
Conservation of atoms and a yield below 100%

No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the calculated amount of product is not always obtained. The atoms still exist, but some are in unreacted reactants, in a different product, or in product that was never collected.

A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is worked out from the balanced equation, so it is a property of the reaction chosen rather than of how well the experiment was carried out.

It is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons to use reactions with high atom economy: less of the starting material ends up as waste that must be treated or disposed of, and less raw material is bought for each tonne of useful product.

(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) x 100. Both figures are read from the balanced equation, including the balancing numbers.

The desired product is the substance the reaction is being carried out to make; any other product is a by-product. Atom economy is always quoted for a stated desired product, so the same reaction has different atom economies depending on which product is wanted.

A number written in front of a formula multiplies the whole of that relative formula mass. In Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 the desired product term is 2 x 56 = 112 and the reactant total is 160 + (3 x 28) = 244.
Theoretical mass from a balanced equation

Divide the given mass of reactant by its relative formula mass, use the balanced equation to convert to the amount of product, then multiply by the relative formula mass of the product. This gives the maximum theoretical mass of that product.

Where more than one reaction makes the same product, the pathway chosen is judged on data such as atom economy, yield, rate, the position of any equilibrium and the usefulness of the by-products, not on any single one of these figures alone.
Percentage yield compared with atom economy

Percentage yield measures how much of the possible product a particular preparation actually delivered. Atom economy measures how much of the starting material the equation itself sends into the desired product. A reaction can be high in one and low in the other.

A by-product that can be sold or used elsewhere means less of the starting material is truly wasted, so a pathway with a modest atom economy may still be chosen. The by-product does not change the atom economy figure for the desired product.

using-concentrations-of-solutions-in-mol.d: Using concentrations of solutions in mol/dm 3 (chemistry only) (HT only)
terms: A measure of how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. The concentration of a solution can be measured in mol/dm³, which states the amount of solute, in moles, present in each 1 dm³ of solution.

The unit 'moles per decimetre cubed'. A concentration of 0.100 mol/dm³ means that every 1 dm³ of the solution contains 0.100 mol of solute. The unit describes the solution as a whole, so any portion taken from it has the same concentration.

The solute is the substance dissolved; the volume used in a concentration in mol/dm³ is the volume of the final solution, not the volume of water added to make it. A solid dissolved and made up to 1 dm³ of solution gives a solution whose volume is 1 dm³.

1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so a volume measured in cm³ is divided by 1000 to give the volume in dm³. For example 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³. Because the unit of concentration is mol/dm³, volumes must be in dm³ before they are used in any concentration calculation.
Amount of solute in a given volume

The amount of solute, in moles, in a given volume of solution is found from the concentration: amount (mol) = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume of solution (dm³). This follows directly from the meaning of mol/dm³ as moles of solute per 1 dm³.
Mass of solute in a given volume

Once the amount of solute in moles is known, its mass is found using the relative formula mass: mass (g) = amount (mol) × relative formula mass. Combining the two steps, mass of solute = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³) × relative formula mass.

The mass of solute dissolved in each 1 dm³ of solution. It is linked to the concentration in mol/dm³ by the relative formula mass: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass. The same concentration in mol/dm³ therefore gives different g/dm³ values for different solutes.
Mole ratio from the balanced equation

The balancing numbers in a balanced symbol equation give the ratio in which the substances react in moles. In H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O the ratio is 1 mol of sulfuric acid to 2 mol of sodium hydroxide, and this ratio converts the known amount of one solute into the amount of the other.

Two solutions react completely when the amounts of the two solutes are in exactly the ratio given by the balanced equation, so neither is left over. Knowing the two volumes that react completely, and the concentration of one solution, fixes the concentration of the other.

For a fixed mass of solute, making the solution up to a larger volume gives a smaller concentration in mol/dm³, because the same amount of solute is spread through more solution. Adding water changes the concentration but not the amount of solute present.

use-of-amount-of-substance-in-relation-t.d: Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)
terms: equal amounts in moles occupy equal volumes

Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure. What fixes the volume of a gas is the number of moles of particles present, not the mass of the sample and not the size of the individual molecules.
The stated conditions of 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure, at which the molar gas volume of 24 dm³ applies. Gas volumes may only be converted using 24 dm³ per mole when the gas is at these conditions.
The volume occupied by one mole of any gas. At room temperature and pressure this is 24 dm³ per mole, so volume in dm³ = amount in mol × 24.
The amount of a substance in moles is found from amount (mol) = mass (g) ÷ relative formula mass. This is the first step in turning a mass of gas into a volume at room temperature and pressure.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in the formula of a substance. For a gas made of molecules such as O2 the whole molecule counts, so Mr(O2) = 32, not 16.
mole ratio from a balanced equation
The balancing numbers in a balanced symbol equation give the ratio of the amounts in moles of the substances that react and that are formed.

Because equal amounts in moles of gases occupy equal volumes under the same conditions, the balancing numbers of the gaseous species also give the ratio of their volumes directly. Volumes of gases may therefore be scaled without converting to moles first, provided every gas involved is at the same temperature and pressure.
changing the subject of an equation

Rearranging a relationship so that the required quantity stands alone on one side. A quantity that multiplies on one side becomes a division when it is moved to the other side, and a quantity that divides becomes a multiplication.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. When a metal reacts with oxygen the metal gains oxygen, so the metal is oxidised.
A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen. When a metal oxide is heated with carbon the oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced.
The compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen, for example magnesium oxide from magnesium burning in air.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together: oxygen lost by one substance is gained by another.
A list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity, deduced from their reactions with water and with dilute acids.
The readiness with which a metal atom loses its outer electrons to become a positive ion. The greater this tendency, the more reactive the metal.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.
Carbon and hydrogen in the series
The two non-metals often included in the reactivity series as reference points; carbon sits between magnesium and zinc, hydrogen between iron and copper.
Reaction of a metal with water
A reaction at room temperature giving a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, shown by potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium, and only very slowly by magnesium.
Reaction of a metal with dilute acid
A reaction giving a salt and hydrogen, shown by magnesium, zinc and iron; copper does not react with dilute acid.
A metal found in the Earth as the element itself rather than as a compound, because it is very unreactive; gold is the standard example.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile.
Heating the oxide of a metal that is less reactive than carbon with carbon, so that the carbon takes the oxygen and the metal is left.
The loss of electrons by a species during a reaction.
The gain of electrons by a species during a reaction.
An equation showing only the species that change in a reaction, with spectator ions left out.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, for example Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
An ion present in the reaction mixture that is unchanged by the reaction and is therefore omitted from the ionic equation.

A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or by another positive ion. The acid supplies the negative ion and the metal, base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive ion.
Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen: for example Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen is seen as bubbles of gas.
Only metals more reactive than hydrogen release hydrogen from a dilute acid. Magnesium, zinc and iron do; copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
Loss of electrons. When a metal reacts with an acid the metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions, so the metal is oxidised.
Gain of electrons. In an acid-metal reaction the hydrogen ions gain electrons to become hydrogen molecules, so they are reduced.
A reaction in which electrons are transferred, so that oxidation and reduction happen together. Acid-metal reactions are redox reactions.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, such as Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ or 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
An ion that is present but unchanged by the reaction, such as the chloride ion when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid.
A substance that neutralises an acid to give a salt and water. Insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides are bases.
A base that dissolves in water, such as a soluble metal hydroxide. Its aqueous solution contains hydroxide ions.
The reaction of an acid with a base, alkali or carbonate in which the acid is used up and a salt is formed.
Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which is why the mixture fizzes.
The salt's name has two parts: the first comes from the positive ion of the base, alkali or carbonate, the second from the acid used.
Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates and sulfuric acid produces sulfates.
The positive ion in a salt comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, not from the acid and not from the water formed.
Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base or alkali gives salt + water; acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Familiar ions used to build salt formulae include Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ and CO₃²⁻.
A salt formula is neutral overall, so the ions are combined in the ratio that cancels the charges, using brackets where a whole ion is repeated, as in Ca(NO₃)₂.
A soluble salt is made by reacting an acid with a solid insoluble metal, metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, then removing the unreacted solid.
Solid is added until no more reacts, which guarantees that all the acid has been used and none is left to contaminate the salt.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper. The unreacted solid stays as the residue; the dissolved salt passes through as the filtrate.
Concentrating a salt solution by evaporating some of the water and then leaving it, so that crystals of the solid salt form as the rest evaporates.
Crystals that contain no unreacted acid or solid and no remaining water; they are patted dry between filter papers rather than heated hard.
Preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate, using a Bunsen burner to heat the dilute acid.
The gentle heating used to evaporate the salt solution in Required practical 1, so that the salt is not decomposed and crystals can form.
The ion that all acids produce in aqueous solution; it is what makes a solution acidic.
The ion present in aqueous solutions of alkalis; it is what makes a solution alkaline.
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring the acidity or alkalinity of a solution, measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.
An instrument that gives a numerical pH reading directly, more precisely than a colour chart can.
A solution with pH 7. Below 7 a solution is acidic, above 7 it is alkaline.
In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, the hydrogen ions from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the alkali to produce water.
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, the equation the specification gives for the reaction of hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions.
A wide range indicator whose colour is matched to a chart to give an approximate pH.
A measured pH is used to classify a solution: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.
A method of measuring the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.
The graduated tube that delivers the solution added a little at a time, read to the nearest 0.05 cm³.
Apparatus that delivers an accurate fixed volume, used with a safety filler to place the alkali in the conical flask.
The moment when the indicator changes colour permanently, showing that the acid and alkali have exactly reacted.
Titres that agree within 0.10 cm³. The rough titre is discarded and the mean is taken from the concordant results.
Amount of substance in moles divided by volume in dm³; volumes in cm³ are divided by 1000 first.
Mass in grams per dm³ of solution; it equals the concentration in mol/dm³ multiplied by Mᵣ.
An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution. Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong acids.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak acids.
The fraction of the acid molecules that have released their hydrogen ions. It is what strong and weak describe.
As pH falls by one unit the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.
A small amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. Dilute is about amount, not about ionisation.
A large amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. A weak acid can still be concentrated.
Comparing solutions by pH: the lower the whole-number pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration, with pH 7 as neutral.
An ionic compound that has been melted or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. Electrolytes conduct electricity.
The process in which passing an electric current through an electrolyte makes the ions move to the electrodes, where they are discharged to produce elements.
The negative electrode. Positively charged ions move to it.
The positive electrode. Negatively charged ions move to it.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not take part in the reactions of the cell, so the products come only from the electrolyte.
The loss of charge by an ion at an electrode, as electrons are gained or lost, turning the ion into a neutral atom or molecule of an element.
An ionic compound made of just two elements, one metal and one non-metal, such as lead bromide or magnesium chloride.
Products of a molten binary compound
When a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed with inert electrodes, the metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Obtaining a metal from its molten compound by electrolysis. It is used when the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, or when the metal reacts with carbon.
Large amounts of energy are used in extraction by electrolysis, both to melt the compound and to produce the electrical current.
The compound mixed with aluminium oxide in the aluminium cell. The mixture melts at a lower temperature than aluminium oxide alone, so less energy is needed.
The positive electrode is made of carbon. Oxygen produced there reacts with the hot carbon, so the electrode is worn away and must be replaced continually.
At the negative electrode hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; otherwise the metal is produced.
At the positive electrode oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.
In an aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, and these ions can be discharged at the electrodes.
A testable idea, put forward before the experiment, that predicts what will happen and can be supported or disproved by the results of Required practical 3.
Gain of electrons. At the cathode positively charged ions gain electrons, so the reactions there are reductions.
Loss of electrons. At the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, so the reactions there are oxidations.
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode only, including the electrons gained or lost, balanced for both atoms and charge.
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, which may also be written as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop with hydrogen. A glowing splint relights in oxygen, and damp litmus paper is bleached by chlorine.

Energy is conserved in chemical reactions: the amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. Energy is only moved between the reacting chemicals and their surroundings.

Everything outside the reacting chemicals themselves, including the solvent, the container and the air. It is the temperature of the surroundings that a thermometer in the reaction mixture actually measures.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. The product molecules end up with less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
The reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy. Combustion is exothermic.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Many oxidation reactions, such as the slow oxidation of iron in a hand warmer, are exothermic.
The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to form a salt and water. Neutralisation is exothermic.
The breaking down of a compound into simpler substances on heating, for example calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Thermal decompositions are endothermic.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: a reaction in a separate compartment of the can transfers energy to the drink and warms it.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: iron powder oxidises slowly inside the pack and transfers energy to the surroundings.
A use of an endothermic reaction: the reaction inside the pack takes in energy from the surroundings, so the pack and the injury are cooled.
The rise or fall in temperature measured before and after a reaction. A rise shows an exothermic reaction; a fall shows an endothermic one.
An investigation of the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, such as acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations and displacement of metals.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy; a collision with too little energy does not lead to a reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
An energy level diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change, with a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products, shown on a reaction profile and, at higher tier, calculated from bond energies.
Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.
Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
The energy associated with a particular bond, used to calculate the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

chemical-cells-and-fuel-cells.d: Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)
terms: A chemical cell contains chemicals which react together to produce electricity. The electricity is not stored inside the cell beforehand: it is produced by the reaction, and only while the reaction can continue and the circuit is complete.

One of the two conducting solids, usually metals, that dip into the electrolyte and are connected into the external circuit. The type of electrode used is one of the factors that determines the voltage a cell produces.
The conducting liquid or paste in which the electrodes are placed. It contains ions that can move, and the type of electrolyte used is one of the factors that determines the voltage a cell produces.

The potential difference produced across the two electrodes of a cell. It depends upon a number of factors, including the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte, not upon how large the cell is.

A cell made by connecting two different metals that are in contact with an electrolyte. The two metals must be different: two identical electrodes react with the electrolyte in the same way and produce no voltage.
Two or more cells connected together in series. Connecting cells in series provides a greater voltage than a single cell, because the voltages of the individual cells add together.
Cells joined end to end so that the same current passes through each one in turn. Joined this way their voltages add, which is why a battery of four 1.5 V cells provides 6.0 V.

A cell in which the chemical reactions cannot be reversed. The reactions stop, and the cell stops producing a voltage, when one of the reactants has been used up. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
The named example of a non-rechargeable battery in this specification. It cannot be recharged: once one of its reactants has been used up the reactions stop and the battery is replaced.

A cell that can be recharged because the chemical reactions inside it are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. No new chemicals are added and no waste is removed; the products are turned back into reactants.

In a cell made from two different metals in an electrolyte, the greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage produced. This allows voltages for untested pairs to be predicted from reactivity data.

A cell that is supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the cell to produce a potential difference, and the cell keeps working for as long as the fuel and oxygen are supplied.

Oxidation carried out at an electrode so that the electrons lost by the fuel travel round the external circuit. This is what allows a fuel cell to produce a potential difference directly, rather than releasing the energy as heat by burning.
The overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Water is the only product of the reaction in the cell.

An equation showing what happens at one electrode, including the electrons. In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte the negative electrode reaction is H2 → 2H+ + 2e− and the positive electrode reaction is O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O. Both atoms and charges must balance.

Weighing advantages against disadvantages using evidence: for cells, cost, lifetime, whether they can be recharged and how they are disposed of; for hydrogen fuel cells, the fact that only water is produced set against the difficulty and cost of storing and distributing hydrogen.
How quickly a reaction proceeds. It can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time.
The average rate over a period of time: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken), or (quantity of product formed) / (time taken).
How much of a starting substance has been consumed in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
How much of a new substance has been made in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s, because a quantity is divided by a time.
At Higher Tier the quantity of reactants may be given in moles, and the rate of reaction is then given in mol/s.
A graph of the quantity of product formed, or of reactant used up, plotted against time. Its steepness at any point shows how fast the reaction is going.
A straight line drawn so that it just touches a curve at one point. Its slope is used as a measure of the rate of reaction at that moment.
The change in the y quantity divided by the change in time along the tangent, calculated as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.
The concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
The amount of a dissolved substance in a given volume of solution. A more concentrated solution has more reactant particles in the same volume.
How tightly gas particles are packed. Raising the pressure of reacting gases puts more particles into the same volume.
The area of solid exposed to the other reactant. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more of it.
The cloudiness of a mixture. A reaction that makes an insoluble solid grows cloudy, and the time for a mark to disappear can be timed.
A testable prediction about how one variable will affect another, which the investigation is then designed to test.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
How many collisions happen each second. Increasing it increases the rate of reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
The surface area of a solid divided by its volume. Smaller pieces of the same mass have a larger surface area to volume ratio.
A simple idea used with collision theory: doubling the number of particles in a given volume roughly doubles the collision frequency, and so roughly doubles the rate.
A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts.
A biological catalyst. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
The route a reaction takes from reactants to products. A catalyst provides a different pathway that has a lower activation energy.
An energy diagram for a reaction. For a catalysed reaction it is drawn with a lower hump, while the reactants and products stay at the same energies.

A reaction in which the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. Once some product has formed it is able to change back into the starting substances, so the change is not a one-way dead end.

The double arrow used to represent a reversible reaction, written A + B ⇌ C + D. It shows that the change can run in the forward direction and in the reverse direction; it does not say how much of each substance is present.
The specification's example of a reversible reaction: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Heating the white solid gives the two gases, and cooling the gases forms the white solid again.

Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate loses water on heating to give white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, taking energy in. Adding water to the white solid gives the blue solid again and releases the same amount of energy.
Apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, so that everything made by the forward reaction stays in the mixture and is available for the reverse reaction.

The state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. Both reactions are still happening, so the amounts of the substances stay constant rather than becoming equal.

A description of the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium. Moving towards the products is called shifting to the right; moving towards the reactants is shifting to the left.

The idea that if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, the system responds to counteract the change. It is used to predict the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium.
The system shifts in the direction that opposes what was done to it, reducing the effect of the change without cancelling it completely, so the new equilibrium is different from the original one.

If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products are formed until equilibrium is reached again; if the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants react until equilibrium is reached again.

Raising the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction and decreases it for an exothermic reaction. Lowering the temperature has the opposite effect in each case.

For gaseous reactions, an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules, and a decrease in pressure shifts it towards the side with the larger number.
Counting molecules from the symbol equation
The numbers of gas molecules on each side of an equilibrium are read from the balancing numbers in the symbol equation, so 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 has three molecules on the left and two on the right.

carbon-compounds-as-fuels-and-feedstock.d: Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock
terms: A finite resource found in rocks; the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
A resource that is being used up far faster than it is formed, so the supply will eventually run out.
Material that was once living. The biomass that formed crude oil consisted mainly of plankton.
Two or more substances that are not chemically joined together. Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds.
A molecule made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
The homologous series that most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to, with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A family of similar compounds that share a general formula, such as the alkanes.
A formula that gives the number of each kind of atom in terms of n. For alkanes it is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A formula such as C₂H₆ that gives the number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
A drawing that shows every atom in a molecule and the covalent bonds between them.
The first alkane, CH₄; one carbon atom joined to four hydrogen atoms.
The second alkane, C₂H₆; two carbon atoms joined to each other and to six hydrogen atoms.
A part of crude oil separated by fractional distillation, containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.
Separating the hydrocarbons in crude oil into fractions by evaporating the oil and condensing each fraction at a different temperature.
Turning a liquid into a vapour. The heated crude oil evaporates before it enters the fractionating column.
Turning a vapour back into a liquid. Each fraction condenses where the column has cooled to its boiling point.
A raw material fed into a chemical process. Crude oil fractions are used as feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
The industry that turns crude oil fractions into useful materials such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. For hydrocarbons it increases as the molecules get larger.
How thick a liquid is and how easily it flows. Hydrocarbons become more viscous as the molecules get larger.
How easily a substance catches fire. Hydrocarbons become less flammable as the molecules get larger.
Burning a fuel in oxygen, which releases energy.
Burning a hydrocarbon in plenty of oxygen so that the only products are carbon dioxide and water.
Gain of oxygen. During combustion both the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised.
Breaking down hydrocarbons to produce smaller, more useful molecules.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
A type of hydrocarbon produced by cracking. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
Adding bromine water to a hydrocarbon. An alkene turns the orange bromine water colourless; an alkane does not.
A very long molecule made by joining many small molecules together. Alkenes are used to produce polymers.

reactions-of-alkenes-and-alcohols.d: Reactions of alkenes and alcohols (chemistry only)
terms: A hydrocarbon with a double carbon-carbon bond. It contains carbon and hydrogen only; the C=C is what separates it from an alkane.
CₙH₂ₙ. Every member has twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms: C₂H₄, C₃H₆, C₄H₈, C₅H₁₀. The alkanes, by contrast, are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Describes a molecule with a carbon-carbon double bond. An alkene is unsaturated because it contains two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.
Describes a molecule in which every carbon-carbon bond is single, so each carbon atom is joined to as many atoms as it can be. The alkanes are saturated.
Ethene (C₂H₄), propene (C₃H₆), butene (C₄H₈) and pentene (C₅H₁₀). The series begins at two carbon atoms because a C=C needs two carbon atoms.
A formula such as C₃H₆ that gives the number of atoms of each element in one molecule. It does not show how the atoms are joined or where the double bond lies.
A drawing showing every atom and every bond in the molecule, so a C=C appears as two lines between two carbon atoms. It carries more information than a molecular formula.
The group of atoms in a molecule that gives a homologous series its characteristic reactions. Members of a series share a functional group and so react in the same ways.
The carbon-carbon double bond, the functional group of the alkenes. It is the site of their addition reactions.
It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds, so ethene, propene, butene and pentene all react in the same ways.
Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions like other hydrocarbons, but tend to burn in air with smoky flames because combustion is incomplete and carbon is released as soot.
A reaction in which atoms add across the carbon-carbon double bond so that the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond. Alkenes react in this way with hydrogen, water and the halogens.
Hydrogen adds across the C=C over a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C, turning the alkene into the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms: ethene gives ethane.
Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of a catalyst, at high temperature and pressure, and water adds across the double bond to give an alcohol: ethene gives ethanol.
Chlorine, bromine or iodine adds across the C=C at room temperature. Bromine water is decolourised, which is the test that tells an alkene from an alkane.
A compound containing the functional group –OH. Alcohols are not hydrocarbons, because they contain oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen.
Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol, the first four members of a homologous series of alcohols.
Ethanol may be written as CH₃CH₂OH, which shows the –OH group and how the carbon atoms are grouped, or drawn as a displayed formula showing every bond.
Sodium reacts with an alcohol, fizzing steadily and releasing hydrogen gas. The reaction is gentler than that of sodium with water.
Alcohols burn in air. Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, for example C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
The first four alcohols dissolve in water, and the solutions formed have a neutral pH.
Warming an alcohol with an oxidising agent produces the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms: ethanol gives ethanoic acid.
The first four alcohols are used as fuels and as solvents; ethanol is also the alcohol in alcoholic drinks.
The process in which aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast.
Yeast is added to an aqueous sugar solution kept warm at about 30 °C with air kept out. Too high a temperature kills the yeast and stops the process.
An alcohol can be picked out from a name ending in -ol, such as butanol, or from a formula containing the –OH group, such as CH₃CH₂OH.
A compound containing the functional group –COOH. Its aqueous solutions are acidic.
Methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid, the first four members of a homologous series of carboxylic acids.
Ethanoic acid may be written as CH₃COOH, which shows the carboxyl group joined to a CH₃ group, or drawn as a displayed formula showing every bond.
The drawing shows the C=O and the O–H of the carboxyl group as separate bonds, which CH₃COOH written on one line does not set out.
A carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate, fizzing as carbon dioxide is given off, in the same way as other acids do.
Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to give acidic solutions with a pH below 7.
A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, in the presence of an acid catalyst, to produce an ester. Ethanoic acid with ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. The carboxylic acids are weak acids.
Because only some molecules ionise, a weak acid solution has a lower concentration of H+ ions, and so a higher pH, than a strong acid of the same concentration.
A carboxylic acid can be picked out from a name ending in -oic acid, such as propanoic acid, or from a formula containing –COOH, such as CH₃COOH.

synthetic-and-naturally-occurring-polyme.d: Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)
terms: A small molecule that joins with many others of the same or a different kind to build a polymer. For addition polymerisation the monomer must contain a C=C double bond.
A very large molecule made when many small monomer molecules join together in a long chain.
A reaction in which many alkene monomers join together to form a polymer, and no other product is formed.
The addition polymer made from ethene, CH₂=CH₂. Its repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–.
The addition polymer made from propene, CH₃CH=CH₂. Its repeating unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
The section of a polymer chain that repeats over and over. In an addition polymer it contains exactly the same atoms as the monomer, with the C=C replaced by a C–C single bond.
The carbon–carbon double bond. Its presence in a molecule shows that the molecule is an alkene and can act as a monomer for addition polymerisation.
The bonds drawn through the brackets of a repeating unit. They show that the unit is joined to further units on both sides in a long chain.
The symbol used for the large number of monomer molecules that react, and for the equally large number of repeating units in the polymer chain formed.
A reaction in which monomers that each carry two functional groups join together, usually losing a small molecule such as water each time a link is made.
The group of atoms in a molecule that decides how that molecule reacts, for example –OH, –COOH, –NH₂ or C=C.
A monomer with two carbon atoms carrying an –OH group on each of them, HOCH₂CH₂OH. It supplies the alcohol groups in a polyester.
A monomer with six carbon atoms carrying a –COOH group at each end, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH. It supplies the acid groups in a polyester.
The link formed when an –OH group and a –COOH group react and a molecule of water is lost. Many ester links along a chain make a polyester.
The condensation polymer formed when a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, such as ethanediol and hexanedioic acid, polymerise together with the loss of water.
A molecule containing two different functional groups, an amino group –NH₂ and a carboxyl group –COOH. Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH.
The condensation polymer formed when many amino acid molecules join together, losing a molecule of water at each link.
A naturally occurring polymer built from different amino acids combined in the same chain.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, a large molecule essential for life that encodes the genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.
The monomer from which DNA is built. Four different nucleotides are used, and most DNA molecules are two chains of them in a double helix.
The shape taken by most DNA molecules, in which two polymer chains are twisted around one another.
A naturally occurring polymer made from glucose monomers, used by plants as an energy store.
A naturally occurring polymer, also made from glucose monomers, that forms plant cell walls.
A polymer made by living things rather than in industry. Examples important for life are DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose.
In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. Purity is a statement about what is in the sample, not about how clean, clear or natural it looks.

Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined. The substances keep their own properties, which is why a mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures rather than at one temperature.

In everyday language a pure substance is one that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk. Such a substance is almost always a mixture in the chemical sense.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes from solid to liquid. A pure substance melts sharply at that one temperature rather than over a range.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes from liquid to gas. A pure liquid boils steadily at that one temperature while it all turns to gas.
Using melting and boiling data to test purity

Compare the measured value with the data book value for the pure substance, and look at whether the change happens at one temperature or over a range. An impurity lowers a melting point and raises a boiling point, and in both cases spreads the change over a range.
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose.

Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Change the proportions and the product no longer does its job properly.
Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. Each is a mixture, so a formulation is never a pure substance.
A technique that can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances. It involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
The phase that does not move. In paper chromatography the paper is the stationary phase, and a substance attracted strongly to it is held back near the origin.
The phase that moves. In paper chromatography the solvent is the mobile phase, and it carries dissolved substances up the paper as it rises.
