Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases. A substance more attracted to the solvent than to the paper spends more time moving and travels further; a substance held more strongly by the paper travels less far.

The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent: R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent). It is a ratio of two distances, so it has no units and is always less than 1.

Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, which can be used to help identify the compounds. The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent, but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents.
The pencil line on which the samples are spotted. The distance moved by a compound is measured from this line to the centre of its spot.
The furthest point the solvent reaches up the paper, marked in pencil as soon as the paper is taken out. The distance moved by the solvent is measured from the origin to this line.
Significant figures in an Rf value

An answer is given to an appropriate number of significant figures, which means no more than the measurements it came from. Distances read to two significant figures give an Rf value quoted to two significant figures.

Investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances, calculating Rf values. The start line is drawn in pencil and the solvent in the container starts below that line.
A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of the gas. A positive result is that the gas burns rapidly with a pop sound.
A wooden splint that has been lit and is still alight. In the hydrogen test it is held at the open end of the test tube, not pushed down into the gas.
The short, sharp sound heard when hydrogen burns rapidly at the mouth of the test tube. It is the observation that identifies hydrogen.
A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of the gas. A positive result is that the splint relights.
A wooden splint that has been lit and then blown out, so that the tip still glows red but has no flame. It is inserted into the test tube of gas.
The glowing splint bursts back into flame when it is inserted into the gas. This observation identifies oxygen.
The gas is shaken with, or bubbled through, limewater. A positive result is that the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide. It is the reagent used in the test for carbon dioxide.
The appearance of the limewater after carbon dioxide has been shaken with it or bubbled through it: the clear, colourless solution becomes a milky white, cloudy liquid.
Litmus paper is used. Damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas; a positive result is that the paper is bleached and turns white.
Litmus paper that has been moistened with water before being put into the gas. The specification states that the litmus paper is damp when the test is carried out.
The colour of the litmus paper is removed, so the paper turns white. This is the observation that identifies chlorine.

identification-of-ions-by-chemical-and-s.d: Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)
terms: A test in which a sample of a compound is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame; some metal ions give the flame a distinctive colour, and that colour identifies the metal ion.
A positively charged ion. The metal ions identified by flame tests and by sodium hydroxide solution are cations.
The flame colour produced by lithium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by sodium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by potassium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by calcium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by copper compounds in a flame test.
When a sample contains a mixture of ions, one strong flame colour can hide, or mask, the colour produced by another metal ion, so that ion is not seen.
Identifying a species from test results
Combining the results of the flame test, the sodium hydroxide test, the carbonate test, the halide test and the sulfate test to name the metal ion and the negative ion, and so the compound.
Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of an unknown salt; the colour of the metal hydroxide precipitate that forms identifies the metal ion.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed. In these tests the precipitate is a metal hydroxide, a silver halide or barium sulfate.
Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
Of the three white hydroxide precipitates, only aluminium hydroxide dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added; this distinguishes aluminium ions from calcium and magnesium ions.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured, not white, precipitates with sodium hydroxide solution.
The blue precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions.
Iron(II) ions give a green precipitate and iron(III) ions give a brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution.
A balanced symbol equation showing a metal salt solution reacting with sodium hydroxide solution to give the insoluble metal hydroxide, for example MgCl2 + 2NaOH -> Mg(OH)2 + 2NaCl.
Adding a dilute acid to the substance; carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas, seen as fizzing.
Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater: the gas is bubbled through limewater, which turns cloudy.
Adding dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution to the solution; halide ions produce a silver halide precipitate.
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution; sulfate ions produce a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
Using chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, covering the ions from the flame tests section through to the sulfates section.
A method of detecting and identifying elements and compounds using a machine rather than a chemical test. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
Compared with the chemical tests in this specification, instrumental methods are more accurate, more sensitive (they detect very small amounts) and faster.
An instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.
In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope; the output is a line spectrum.
A set of results for known substances, in the same chart or tabular form as the sample result, against which an instrumental result is compared to identify the ions present.

composition-and-evolution-of-the-earths-.d: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
terms: For the last 200 million years the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today. The atmosphere has therefore been broadly stable over that period, but was very different before it.
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere. It is the most abundant gas in the air today.
Oxygen makes up about one-fifth (approximately 20%) of the atmosphere. It is the second most abundant gas in the air today.

The remainder of the atmosphere is made up of small proportions of various other gases, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases. Together these account for only a small proportion of the air.
Why evidence for the early atmosphere is limited

Evidence for the Earth's early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years. Scientists cannot sample an atmosphere that existed billions of years ago, so conclusions rest on indirect evidence.

Theories about what was in the Earth's early atmosphere and how the atmosphere was formed have changed and developed over time. A theory is the current best explanation of the available evidence and is revised as new evidence is found.
One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence there was intense volcanic activity that released the gases which formed the early atmosphere.
The same volcanic activity released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.
At the start of this period the Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere. Because nitrogen is unreactive it was not readily removed, so its proportion increased over time.
There may also have been small proportions of methane and ammonia in the early atmosphere.
When the oceans formed, carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments. This reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Evaluating theories about the early atmosphere

Given appropriate information, students should be able to interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the Earth's early atmosphere, judging how far the evidence supports a claim and where its limitations lie.

Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, which can be represented by the equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, that is, carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere. Over the next billion years plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
Algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, because the reaction uses carbon dioxide as a reactant.
Carbon locked into rocks and fuels

Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon. Carbon taken from the atmosphere by living organisms was buried and retained in these deposits.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, which are made of calcium carbonate. These deposits built up on the sea bed and were buried and compressed, locking carbon into the rock.

Coal is a sedimentary rock formed from thick deposits of plant material. The plants were buried by sediment and, over millions of years, heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen converted the deposits to coal.
Formation of crude oil and natural gas

Crude oil and natural gas were formed from the remains of plankton (marine organisms) that were buried in mud on the sea bed and changed over millions of years by heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen.
Main changes in the atmosphere over time

The main changes are a large decrease in carbon dioxide and an increase in oxygen. Carbon dioxide fell because it dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonates, was used in photosynthesis, and was locked into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels; oxygen rose because algae and then plants photosynthesised.

carbon-dioxide-and-methane-as-greenhouse.d: Carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases
terms: A gas in the atmosphere that absorbs long wavelength radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-radiates some of it back towards the Earth. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
The specification names water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). Nitrogen and oxygen, which together make up about 99% of the air, are not greenhouse gases.
The process by which greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life. Without it the Earth's surface would be far colder.
Radiation from the Sun. Most of it passes through the atmosphere without being absorbed by greenhouse gases and is absorbed by the Earth's surface, warming it.
Radiation emitted by the warmed Earth's surface. Its wavelength is longer than that of the radiation arriving from the Sun, and greenhouse gases absorb it.
Greenhouse gases absorb long wavelength radiation from the Earth and re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the surface, so the surface stays warmer.
Burning fossil fuels (in power stations, vehicles and homes) and deforestation, which leaves fewer trees to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Cattle and other livestock farming, and the decay of organic waste in landfill sites. Growing rice in flooded paddy fields also releases methane.
Checking of a scientist's methods, data and conclusions by other scientists working in the same field before the work is published.
The evidence for climate change does not fix a single exact outcome: measurements have limits, the climate system is complex and future emissions are unknown, so predictions are given as ranges.
A report presents only part of the evidence, or presents opinion or speculation as if it were established evidence, often to support a particular point of view.
A long-term change in the Earth's climate, caused mainly by an increase in the average global temperature of the atmosphere at the surface.
Sea level rise and flooding of low-lying land, more frequent and severe storms, changes to the amount and distribution of rainfall, and changes to the range of many wild species.
Risk combines how likely an effect is with how severe it would be. Climate change is global in scale, so the effects and the risks are not confined to the countries that emit the most.
The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
Every stage from obtaining raw materials, through manufacture, transport and use, to disposal at the end of the product's useful life.
Using renewable energy or nuclear power, increasing energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage, carbon taxes and licences, and capturing methane from landfill and livestock.
Cost, the slow pace of scientific and technological development, disagreement between governments, lack of public information and education, and reluctance to change lifestyles.

common-atmospheric-pollutants-and-their-.d: Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
terms: The burning of a fuel in oxygen, which releases energy. The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
A substance released into the atmosphere that harms human health or the environment. Burning fuels is a major source of these substances.
Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen. Some fuels also contain a small amount of sulfur.
Sulfur is present as an impurity in some fuels, such as coal. It is not a part of every fuel, so not every fuel produces sulfur dioxide when it burns.
Burning in a plentiful supply of oxygen. Carbon in the fuel is oxidised to carbon dioxide and hydrogen in the fuel is oxidised to water vapour.

Burning when the supply of oxygen is too small for the fuel to burn completely. As well as carbon dioxide and water vapour, carbon monoxide, solid carbon particles (soot) and unburned hydrocarbons may be released.
Carbon monoxide, CO, is produced when a fuel containing carbon burns in a supply of oxygen that is too small for complete combustion, so the carbon is only partly oxidised.
Soot is solid particles of carbon released when a fuel burns in too little oxygen and some of the carbon in the fuel is not oxidised at all.
Sulfur present as an impurity in the fuel is oxidised when the fuel burns: S + O2 → SO2. Fuels with no sulfur in them do not produce sulfur dioxide.
How oxides of nitrogen are produced
At the high temperatures reached inside an engine, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together to form oxides of nitrogen. The nitrogen comes from the air, not from the fuel.
Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons released when a fuel is burned form particulates in the atmosphere.
Fuel molecules that leave the engine or burner without reacting. Together with solid particles they form particulates in the atmosphere.

Work from two pieces of information: which elements the fuel contains, and how much oxygen is available. Carbon gives carbon dioxide, and also carbon monoxide and carbon particles if oxygen is limited; hydrogen gives water vapour; sulfur gives sulfur dioxide; a high temperature in air gives oxides of nitrogen.
Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas. It is colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected.
Rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen released into the atmosphere when fuels are burned.
Breathing problems caused in humans by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen in the air.
A reduction in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, caused by particulates in the atmosphere.
As well as causing global dimming, particulates in the air cause health problems for humans.

using-the-earths-resources-and-obtaining.d: Using the Earth's resources and obtaining potable water
terms: Anything taken from the Earth, the oceans or the atmosphere that people use. Humans use the Earth's resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport, and natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.

A resource that is not being replaced, or is being replaced far more slowly than it is used, so the supply available on Earth will eventually run out. Crude oil, natural gas and metal ores are finite.
A resource that is replaced at the same rate as, or faster than, it is used, so it can be re-formed within a human lifetime. Timber from managed woodland and cotton are renewable.
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

A product made by an industrial chemical process rather than taken directly from a living thing, made to supplement or replace a natural product, for example synthetic rubber in place of latex from rubber trees.
A product obtained by deliberately farming plants or animals, which supplements the supply obtained from wild natural sources, for example farmed timber, wool and cotton.
A factor of ten. Two quantities differ by one order of magnitude if one is about ten times the other, and by three orders of magnitude if one is about a thousand times the other.
Water that is safe to drink. For humans, drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.
In the chemical sense, water containing only H2O and nothing else. Potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.
Water with low levels of dissolved substances. In the UK rain provides fresh water that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers.
Beds of sand and gravel that water is passed through during treatment so that insoluble solids and larger particles are removed.
Treating water so that microbes in it are killed, making the water safe to drink.
A treatment used to kill microbes in water. Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
Removing dissolved salts from salty water or sea water so that it can be used as potable water. It may be required if supplies of fresh water are limited.
Boiling water and condensing the vapour, so that the water separates from the dissolved solids, which stay behind. One route to desalination and the purification step of Required practical 8.
A desalination process that forces salty water through a membrane which holds back the dissolved ions and lets water through.
Fresh water that has collected in the ground, one of the appropriate sources of fresh water chosen in the UK.
Water containing high levels of dissolved salts, such as sea water, which needs desalination rather than simple filtering and sterilising.
The solid substances dissolved in a water sample, found in Required practical 8 by evaporating a measured volume to dryness and weighing the residue.
Water that has been used by homes, businesses, farms or industry and requires treatment before being released into the environment.
Waste water from homes and businesses containing organic matter and harmful microbes, which must be removed before release.
The first stage of sewage treatment, in which large solid objects and grit are removed from the incoming waste water.
Allowing sewage to stand so that solids settle out as sewage sludge, leaving liquid effluent above them.
The settled solid produced by sedimentation, which is treated by anaerobic digestion.
The liquid produced by sedimentation, which is treated by aerobic biological treatment.
Breakdown of sewage sludge by microorganisms in the absence of oxygen.
Treatment of effluent by microorganisms supplied with air, so that they break down the remaining organic matter.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile. The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited.
Rock that contains only a small percentage of a metal compound, too little for traditional extraction to be worthwhile.
Using plants to absorb metal compounds. The plants are harvested and then burned to produce ash that contains metal compounds.
Using bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.
The solution produced by bioleaching, which contains dissolved metal compounds.
Obtaining copper from a solution of a copper compound by adding a more reactive metal such as scrap iron, which takes the place of the copper.

An assessment of the environmental impact of a product in each of four stages: extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation during its lifetime; and disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

The first LCA stage. It covers obtaining the raw material from the Earth or from living things and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, for example mining an ore and reducing it to the metal, or drilling for crude oil and processing it into a polymer.
The second LCA stage. It covers shaping and assembling the product from the processed material and also the packaging placed around it, including the resources and energy used to make that packaging.
Use and operation during its lifetime

The third LCA stage. It covers everything consumed while the product is in service, such as electricity, fuel, water or detergent, and any maintenance or replacement parts needed over the product's working life.
Disposal at the end of its useful life

The fourth LCA stage. It covers what happens to the product when it is no longer used: collection, landfill, incineration or processing for recycling, together with the resources and energy those routes consume.

The movement of materials, parts, products and wastes. It is not a fifth stage of an LCA; it is counted within each of the four stages, so the fuel used to carry ore to a works and the fuel used to carry waste to landfill are both included.
Use of water, resources and energy sources, and the production of some wastes, can be fairly easily quantified because they can be weighed, metered or measured directly and reported as numbers.

A decision about how much weight to give an effect that cannot simply be measured. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires such judgements, which is why an LCA is not a purely objective process and why two assessors can reach different conclusions from the same data.
A shortened life cycle assessment that considers only some stages, or only some impacts, of a product rather than the whole life cycle.

A conclusion chosen before the assessment is carried out. A selective or abbreviated LCA can be misused by picking the stages and impacts that support such a conclusion, for example to back up a claim made for advertising purposes.

An assessment that sets the life cycle impacts of two products side by side, stage by stage, so they can be compared fairly. A simple example is comparing a shopping bag made from plastic with one made from paper.
The total life cycle impact of a product divided by the number of times it is used. Reusing a shopping bag many times spreads the impact of making it over many uses, so the impact per use falls.
Reduction in use, reuse and recycling

The three actions by end users named in the specification. Together they reduce the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts. Using less in the first place saves the most, because it avoids all four life cycle stages.

A raw material of which the Earth holds a finite amount, so supplies are used up far faster than they form. Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials, and much of the energy for the processes also comes from limited resources.
Environmental impacts of quarrying and mining

Obtaining raw materials from the Earth causes impacts such as loss of habitat, dust, noise, spoil heaps and polluted water, alongside the energy used by the machinery and the transport of the material away from the site.
Using a product again for the same or another purpose without reprocessing the material it is made from. A glass bottle that is collected, washed and refilled has been reused.

Processing a used material so that it can be made into something new. Glass bottles that cannot be refilled are crushed and melted to make different glass products; products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use.
Metals are recycled by melting them and then recasting or reforming the metal into different products, which avoids extracting the same mass of metal from its ore.

Sorting scrap into separate metals or materials before it is melted. The amount of separation required depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product, so some uses need carefully sorted scrap and others do not.
Scrap steel in iron and steel making
Some scrap steel can be added to the iron from a blast furnace. This reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore, so less ore is mined and less ore has to be reduced.
Evaluating ways of reducing resource use

Weighing up options such as reducing use, reuse and recycling using the information given: how much of a limited resource and how much energy each option saves, how much waste it avoids, and what it costs or requires in return.
The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. It is a chemical change, not simply wear, and it is not confined to metals.
The corrosion of iron. It is one example of corrosion, and both air and water must be present for it to happen.
A layer applied to a metal that keeps air and water away from the surface, for example grease, paint or an electroplated layer of another metal.
Using electricity to deposit a thin layer of one metal onto the surface of another, used here as a way of applying a protective barrier.
The thin layer of oxide that forms on the surface of aluminium and protects the metal underneath from further corrosion.
Protecting a metal by putting it in contact with a more reactive metal, which corrodes in its place.
Coating iron or steel with zinc. The zinc acts as a barrier and, because it is more reactive than iron, also gives sacrificial protection.
Fair test in a rusting experiment
Setting up tubes that differ in only one factor - air present or absent, water present or absent - so that any difference in rusting can be traced to that one factor.
A substance such as anhydrous calcium chloride that removes water vapour, used to give a nail air without water.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Most metals in everyday use are alloys because the mixture has more useful properties than the pure metal.
An alloy of copper and tin, used for statues, ornaments and bells.
An alloy of copper and zinc, used for musical instruments, door fittings and taps.
Gold mixed with silver, copper and zinc, which is harder and cheaper than pure gold.
The unit used for the proportion of gold in an alloy. 24 carat is 100% gold and 18 carat is 75% gold.
An alloy of iron containing specific amounts of carbon and, in some steels, other metals.
Steel with a higher proportion of carbon. It is strong but brittle, so it is used for cutting tools and blades.
Steel with a lower proportion of carbon. It is softer and more easily shaped, so it is used for car bodies and sheeting.
Steel containing chromium and nickel. It is hard and resistant to corrosion, so it is used for cutlery, sinks and surgical tools.
An alloy of aluminium. Aluminium alloys are low density, so they are used for aircraft bodies and bicycle frames.
The glass in ordinary use, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Glass made from sand and boron trioxide. It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
A material such as pottery or brick, made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace.
The small molecule from which a polymer is built. Ethene is the monomer for poly(ethene).
Low density poly(ethene), made from ethene under one set of conditions with one catalyst. It is flexible and used for bags and bottles.
High density poly(ethene), made from the same monomer, ethene, but with a different catalyst and different conditions. It is stiffer and stronger.
A polymer made of separate tangled chains held to each other only by weak forces, so it melts when heated and can be reshaped.
A polymer whose chains are joined by cross-links. It does not melt when heated, so it keeps its shape at high temperature.
Strong bonds joining one polymer chain to another, which stop the chains moving past each other on heating.
A material made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of a second material.
The material in a composite that surrounds and holds the reinforcement, for example the cement in concrete.
The fibres or fragments held inside the matrix of a composite, for example the gravel in concrete or the glass fibres in fibreglass.
Mass per unit volume. A low density material has a small mass for its size, which is why aluminium alloys suit aircraft.

the-haber-process-and-the-use-of-npk-fer.d: The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)
terms: The industrial process that manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. The purified gases are passed over an iron catalyst at about 450 degrees C and about 200 atmospheres.
The compound NH3 made by the Haber process. It is the starting point for nitrogen-based fertilisers, and is not itself spread on fields as the finished fertiliser.
A substance fed into an industrial process. For the Haber process the raw materials are the two reactant gases, nitrogen and hydrogen.
The nitrogen for the Haber process comes from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen.
The hydrogen for the Haber process is obtained from natural gas (methane) or other hydrocarbons.
The catalyst used in the Haber process. It speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not change the position of equilibrium, so it does not change the yield.

A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. In the Haber process some of the ammonia formed breaks down again into nitrogen and hydrogen, so the reaction never goes to completion.
Word equation for the Haber process
The specification states the reaction as: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ ammonia. The double arrow shows that the reaction is reversible.
On cooling, the ammonia condenses to a liquid at a much higher temperature than nitrogen or hydrogen do, so it can be run off and removed while the other two gases stay as gases.
The nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted are passed back into the reactor instead of being wasted, which raises the overall conversion and cuts costs.
How quickly ammonia is produced. Raising the temperature, raising the pressure and adding the iron catalyst all increase the rate.
The state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia stay constant although both reactions continue.

How far the equilibrium lies towards the products. Raising the pressure moves it towards ammonia because there are fewer gas molecules on the ammonia side; raising the temperature moves it away from ammonia because the forward reaction is exothermic.
The proportion of the nitrogen and hydrogen that is converted into ammonia at equilibrium. A high yield and a high rate need opposite temperatures, which is why a compromise is needed.

The conditions actually used in industry: about 450 degrees C gives a lower yield than a cool reactor would but a workable rate, and about 200 atmospheres gives a lower yield than very high pressure would but avoids the cost and danger of stronger plant.
A fertiliser containing compounds of all three of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, the elements with symbols N, P and K.
A mixture made in fixed proportions so that it does a job. An NPK fertiliser is a formulation of several salts blended to give appropriate percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
A salt made by reacting ammonia with an acid, for example ammonium nitrate from ammonia and nitric acid, or ammonium sulfate from ammonia and sulfuric acid.
An acid manufactured from ammonia. It is used both to make ammonium nitrate and to treat phosphate rock.
A mined rock containing insoluble phosphate compounds. It supplies phosphorus but cannot be used directly as a fertiliser.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are dug out of the ground rather than synthesised. The potassium salts can be used in fertilisers without further reaction.
A fertiliser has to dissolve in water in the soil before a plant root can take it up, which is why insoluble phosphate rock is first converted into soluble salts.
The mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate made by treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid.
The calcium phosphate made by treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid.

A laboratory preparation is a batch: one small quantity is made, filtered and crystallised by hand. Industrial fertiliser production runs continuously on a large scale through several integrated processes.
The tiny particle from which all matter is composed. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can still exist as that element.
A substance made of only one type of atom. There are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, and each type of atom is an element; the elements are set out in the periodic table.

A substance containing the atoms of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. Because about 100 elements can combine in an enormous number of ratios and arrangements, millions of different compounds exist.

The pattern by which similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals when the elements are arranged in order of atomic number. This repeating pattern is what the word 'periodic' in periodic table refers to.
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which is why they have similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied electron shells, and their properties change steadily across the row rather than staying similar.

The arrangement of the electrons in shells around the nucleus of an atom. It is this arrangement, and above all the number of electrons in the outer shell, that explains the periodic properties of the elements.

Bonding formed when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The oppositely charged ions produced are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction acting in all directions.
Bonding formed when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons. The shared pair is attracted to both nuclei at once, which is what holds the atoms together, and covalent bonds are strong.
An atom, or a group of atoms, that has lost or gained electrons and so carries an overall electrical charge. Losing electrons gives a positive ion; gaining electrons gives a negative ion.
A group of atoms bonded together by covalent bonds. The size and shape of a molecule, and the strength of the forces between one molecule and the next, affect how the substance behaves.

A structure in which very large numbers of atoms or ions are joined by a regular repeating network of strong bonds. Giant ionic lattices, giant covalent structures such as diamond and graphite, and metals are all giant structures.

The idea that the way the particles of a substance are arranged, and the strength of the forces holding them in place, decide its properties - its melting and boiling points, its hardness, and whether it conducts electricity.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react when they collide. It is the barrier to reaction: collisions with less than this energy do not lead to any chemical change.

How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Because different reactions have different energy barriers, and because conditions such as temperature, concentration and surface area differ, reactions occur at very different rates.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. A catalyst is not used up during the reaction.

A chemical change in which a hydrogen ion, H+, is passed from one substance to another. A hydrogen ion is a hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron, so it is a single proton; acid reactions with alkalis and bases work this way.
A chemical change in which electrons pass from one substance to another. Loss of electrons is oxidation and gain of electrons is reduction; the reaction of a metal with a non-metal works this way.
A chemical change in which atoms form covalent bonds by sharing pairs of electrons, rather than by giving electrons up or taking them. Reactions between non-metal elements work this way.

The principle that energy can be neither created nor destroyed. In a chemical reaction energy is only transferred, so the total amount of energy before the reaction equals the total amount afterwards.

An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature falls. In neither case is energy made or lost.
The three ways reactions take place

Chemical reactions take place in only three different ways: proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing. The many familiar names for reactions describe patterns, but underneath each is one of these three changes.

the-composition-and-evolution-of-the-ear.d: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
terms: For the last 200 million years the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today. Before that period the atmosphere was very different.
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths, approximately 80%, of the atmosphere. It is the most abundant gas in the air.
Oxygen makes up about one-fifth, approximately 20%, of the atmosphere.
The remaining small proportions of the atmosphere are various other gases, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases such as argon.

Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years. Theories about what the early atmosphere contained, and how it formed, have therefore changed and developed over time.
Volcanic activity and the early atmosphere
One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence intense volcanic activity released the gases that formed the early atmosphere, together with water vapour.
Water vapour released by the volcanoes condensed to form the oceans.
At the start of that period the Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere. There may also have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.
Carbon dioxide dissolving in the oceans
When the oceans formed, carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated producing sediments, which reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Evaluating theories about the early atmosphere
Given appropriate information, evidence about the early atmosphere can be interpreted and competing theories evaluated by judging how well each one accounts for that evidence.
Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen, or 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere. Over the next billion years plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
Algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, because carbon dioxide is a reactant.
Carbon locked into rocks and fuels
Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, which are made of carbonate and were deposited on the sea bed.
Coal is a sedimentary rock formed from thick layers of plant material buried in swamps, where a lack of oxygen prevented full decay.
Formation of crude oil and natural gas
Crude oil and natural gas formed from the remains of plankton that were buried in mud on the sea bed and altered by heat and pressure over millions of years.

yield-and-atom-economy-of-chemical-react.d: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
terms: The mass of product that would form if every reactant particle reacted exactly as the balanced equation shows and none of the product was lost. It is the largest mass that could possibly be made, so it is the figure the mass actually obtained is compared with.
Conservation of mass in a reaction

No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction. A shortfall on the balance therefore never means that atoms have disappeared; it means atoms are somewhere other than in the product that was collected and weighed.

A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. Such a reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is always still present and the amount of product obtained is below the theoretical maximum.

Product left behind when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example crystals clinging to the filter paper or the beaker, or solid still dissolved in the liquid poured away. It was made but never weighed, so the yield falls.

A reaction in which some of the reactants react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming a substance other than the desired product. The atoms are all still present but they are locked into the wrong compound.
The amount of a product obtained from a reaction. It is a measured quantity, found by weighing the product after it has been separated from the mixture, washed and dried.
The amount of product obtained compared with the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage: % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100.
Finding a theoretical mass from the balanced equation

Convert the given mass of reactant to moles, use the balancing numbers in the equation to find the moles of the desired product, then multiply by the relative formula mass of that product. The balancing numbers must be used or the answer is out by that factor.

A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is worked out from the balanced equation alone, using relative formula masses, so it is fixed for a given reaction whatever happens in the laboratory.
Why a high atom economy matters

A reaction with a high atom economy turns more of the starting materials into the product that is wanted. This is important for sustainable development, because raw materials are limited and waste has to be dealt with, and for economic reasons, because unused starting material and waste disposal both cost money.

(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) x 100. Every reactant in the equation counts in the bottom line, each multiplied by its balancing number.
